title: Habakkuk: by faithfulness (Habakkuk 2:4)
hook: the Talmud says Habakkuk reduced the whole Torah to one line: the righteous live by faith (Makkot 24a)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a fig tree and no fear. Your line was none shall make them afraid. Today, a prophet who opens with a complaint.

"O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" That's how Habakkuk begins, in the King James. Not with a message for the people, but with the prophet arguing upward. He sees violence and strife, the law gone slack, the wicked hemming in the righteous, and he asks why God lets him watch it. The answer troubles him more, so he asks again. Then he does something stubborn. He climbs up to wait: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower." He's not coming down until he hears back.
screen: `HOW LONG SHALL I CRY?` → `THE ANSWER TROUBLES HIM MORE.` → `UP THE TOWER, TO WAIT.`

segments.voice: The answer starts with instructions about handwriting. "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it." Big letters, so even someone running past can read them. Then a warning about time: "though it tarry, wait for it." Then the line: "the just shall live by his faith." The Hebrew word under faith is emunah. In English, faith can sound like a belief you hold in your head. Emunah leans toward something you do with your whole life: steadiness, firmness, keeping faith. The same word turns up in Exodus, when Moses holds up his arms through a long battle and Aaron and Hur prop them up. The King James says his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. Steady: that's emunah. And notice the small word his. Some readers hear the righteous person's own steadiness. Others hear God's faithfulness, the thing the righteous lean on while they wait. The Hebrew can carry both. Now the Talmud. In tractate Makkot, Rabbi Simlai teaches that Moses was given six hundred thirteen commandments, and later voices gathered them into fewer and fewer lines. David set them on eleven, Isaiah on six, Micah on three, Isaiah again on two. For the last step the rabbis weigh Amos, then settle on this: Habakkuk came and set them all on one. The righteous shall live by his faith. Not a rule about food or Shabbat, but the ground every rule stands on, written large enough to read on the run.
screen: `WRITE IT PLAIN, TO READ ON THE RUN.` · `THOUGH IT TARRY, WAIT FOR IT.` · then, large: `THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY HIS FAITH.` · then: `EMUNAH: STEADY HANDS TILL SUNSET.` · then: `ALL OF IT, SET ON ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're waiting on, an answer, a result, a door to open, and like Habakkuk on the tower, choose to stand where you are rather than run. Pick one steady thing you can trust, a person who has kept their word, a habit that holds you, or, if you pray, God's faithfulness, and let his words ride the breath: though it tarry, wait for it.
Habakkuk. The prophet who argued, climbed the tower to wait, and heard the one line that holds up the rest. Today's word.
Your line: live by faithfulness. Steady, until the going down of the sun. That's day eight hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews read Habakkuk among the Twelve, and the Talmud's tractate Makkot names Habakkuk 2:4 as the single line on which the commandments stand.

chat.says: What does 'the just shall live by his faith' mean? Just believing the right things?
options: Emunah means steadiness: living faithfully, like steady hands held up until sunset.
It means only prophets live by faith; everyone else just lives by the rules.
It means the righteous never have to wait, because God answers right away.
